Longitudinal Mixed-Model Calibration Simulation (Goal 5a)

mlmRev::egsingle two-stage hierarchical plasmode resampling

2026-09-25

1 Purpose

This report documents Goal 5a of the RESI mixed-model extension project (see instructions/instructions.md and log/claudeLog.md at the repository root): a calibration check of the simulation machinery for lme4::lmer before any RESI confidence-interval theory is layered on top. It collects, in one place: the dataset used, the simulation settings, the diagnostics that identified a fixed-effect SE mis-calibration under full bootstrap resampling of the real data, and the hybrid plasmode simulation, which is now the primary validation method for calibration going forward (see the note below).

2 Note: full bootstrap (plasmode) resampling does not produce consistent SEs

Earlier work in this project ran longitudinalCalibrationSim(), which resamples the real egsingle data with a two-stage with-replacement cluster bootstrap (draw schools with replacement, then draw children with replacement within each drawn school) and refits Model A/B on each resampled dataset. That full-bootstrap approach produced fixed-effect model-based standard errors that were not consistent with the true (Monte Carlo) sampling variability of the estimates: mean_model_se / mc_sd plateaued well below 1 for child- and occasion-level covariates (female, black, hispanic, year), and the between-school variance component (var_schoolid) showed substantial, growing bias as the number of resampled schools grew. This pattern held on both the real data and a synthetic dataset generated from the same fitted model, and was not fully resolved by decoupling the number of sites from the number of subjects per site (see the diagnostic sections below for that history).

Simon’s hypothesis: this failure is caused by real slope variation across the sampling levels (e.g. schools and children have their own, slightly different coefficients for covariates such as year, female, black, hispanic) that is not included in the model formula (Model A only has random intercepts, not random slopes, for these covariates). When the real data is resampled with replacement, this unmodeled cross-level slope heterogeneity is present in every replicate and inflates the true sampling variability of the fixed-effect estimates beyond what the fitted model’s SE formula – which assumes the random-intercept-only structure is correct – can capture. This is consistent with the slope-heterogeneity diagnostic below, which found that removing true slope heterogeneity from the data-generating process (a synthetic outcome simulated directly from Model A’s own fitted parameters, with no unmodeled heterogeneity by construction) recovers correct SE calibration.

Going forward, the hybrid plasmode simulation (BLUP-resampled random effects; see the dedicated section below) is the primary method used to validate calibration. It keeps a fixed covariate design (so no unmodeled cross-level slope heterogeneity can enter) while still using empirically estimated (resampled, rescaled) random effects rather than a fully parametric Normal draw, and it reproduces correct SE calibration. The raw full-bootstrap plasmode results and code are no longer included in this report; they remain available in tests/ and RESI/R/simulations.R for reference if needed.

3 Dataset: mlmRev::egsingle

egsingle is a 3-level growth-curve dataset (measurement occasion nested in child nested in school) used as the plasmode base because it is the only dataset found (across lme4, nlme, geepack, mlmRev, JM, joineR, merTools) with >=1000 independent subjects, a continuous repeated-measures outcome, and a continuous time covariate suitable for a smooth term.

Every one of the 60 schools has at least 5 children, up to 89, with a mean of 28.7 and median of 24 children per school (SD 18.1) – a right-skewed, moderately variable cluster-size distribution, which is why the plasmode resampling below draws each school’s own number of children (not a fixed number) when it is resampled.

3.3 Variables

egsingle variables and nesting structure
Variable Level Type Description

childid 2 (child, n=1721) factor child identifier, nested in school

retained 1 (occasion) binary factor held back a grade (mostly time-invariant)

black 2 (child) binary factor child race indicator
hispanic 2 (child) binary factor child ethnicity indicator
size 3 (school) continuous school enrollment size
lowinc 3 (school) continuous % low income at school
mobility 3 (school) continuous % student mobility at school

4 Simulation design

4.1 Fixed-divisor covariate rescaling

size (school enrollment, range 113-1486, SD 312.6) is on a very different scale from the other covariates and caused an lme4 convergence warning when used raw. Both size and lowinc are rescaled by a fixed divisor (not a z-score), applied identically to every replicate, so coefficients stay directly interpretable:

  • size_100 = size / 100 (school enrollment in hundreds of students)
  • lowinc_10 = lowinc / 10 (percent low-income in units of 10 percentage points)

Combined with lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 2e5)), both models below fit with 0 convergence warnings on the full data.

4.2 Models A and B

Shared fixed effects: math ~ year + female + black + hispanic + size_100 + lowinc_10

  • Model A (random intercepts only): `+ (1 | schoolid/childid)`
  • Model B (random slope for year at the child level): `+ (1 + year | childid) + (1 | schoolid)`

All models are fit with REML = FALSE (maximum likelihood), since the full-data fit’s fixed effects and variance components are used as the “truth”/population target that each replicate is compared against (the same convention insurancePlasmodeSim()/simCalibrationSim() use for lm/glm).

4.3 Two-stage hierarchical plasmode resampling (deprecated)

An earlier version of this simulation resampled the real data directly in two stages (schools with replacement, then children with replacement within each drawn school). As documented in the note above, this full-bootstrap approach does not produce fixed-effect SEs consistent with the true sampling variability, so it is no longer used for calibration; see RESI/R/simulations.R (.longSimResampleHierarchical()) for the implementation if needed for reference.

Random-effect (variance component) standard errors are not computed by any of the simulations below; only fixed-effect model-based SEs are compared against the Monte Carlo SD of each fixed effect across replicates. Variance-component point estimates are still tracked for bias.

5 Slope-heterogeneity diagnostic (synthetic DGP)

5.1 Motivation and method

Hypothesis: minor real variation in schools’ own coefficients for covariates other than the intercept (which Model A cannot model, since it only has random intercepts) is being absorbed into the fixed-effect sampling variability, causing the SE mis-calibration under full bootstrap resampling described in the note above (this is Simon’s hypothesis for that failure).

Test: tests/test_egsingle_synthetic_calibration.R fits Model A once to the real data to obtain the fixed effects, school-intercept variance, child-intercept variance, and residual variance. For each of 1000 replicates and each requested n_schools, it keeps a deterministic covariate design, draws fresh school random intercepts from \(N(0, \widehat{\sigma}^2_{school})\), draws fresh child random intercepts from \(N(0, \widehat{\sigma}^2_{child})\), and draws fresh observation errors from \(N(0, \widehat{\sigma}^2_e)\). It then constructs \(math = X\widehat{\beta} + b_{school} + b_{child} + e\) and fits Model A. There is no site or subject resampling in this synthetic simulation. When n_schools exceeds the 60 observed site covariate patterns, the fixed design cycles those patterns and re-keys the generated sites; this is a design choice, not random resampling.

5.2 Results

Model A refit on the synthetic (zero true slope heterogeneity) dataset: fixed-effect bias, SE calibration, and variance-component bias vs. n_schools.

5.3 Interpretation

  • Fixed-effect SE calibration is largely recovered. Across n_schools = 15, 30, 60, 90, 120, the corrected fresh-DGP se_ratio is approximately 0.83-1.05 for the fixed effects, including year, female, black, and hispanic; there is no persistent decline like the earlier resampling-based synthetic results.
  • The remaining mild deviations from 1 are ordinary finite-Monte-Carlo and finite-design effects, especially for the intercept and school-level covariates at n_schools = 15; they are not the earlier severe child/occasion-level pattern.
  • Variance-component estimates are close for the child and residual terms. The school variance has positive relative bias at smaller site counts (about 33% at 15 sites, 15% at 30, and 9% at 60), then stabilizes around 8-9% for 90 and 120 sites. This is a separate variance-component estimation issue, not evidence that the fixed-effect SEs are wrong.

6 Sample-size (n_schools vs. n_per_site) diagnostic

6.1 Motivation and method

The corrected fixed-site-size simulation (tests/test_egsingle_synthetic_fixed_n.R) uses the same direct DGP generation, but constructs a deterministic covariate design with exactly n_per_site child profiles per site. For each of the 12 grid cells (n_schools in {15, 30, 60} x n_per_site in {25, 50, 100, 200}) and each of 1000 replicates, it draws fresh school effects, fresh child effects, and fresh residual errors from the fitted Normal variance components, constructs the outcome from the fixed effects plus those draws, and fits Model A. It does not sample sites or subjects with replacement.

6.3 Interpretation

  • Fixed-effect SE calibration is approximately correct across the entire grid. The fresh-DGP se_ratio values for year, female, black, and hispanic are about 0.94-1.07 across all combinations of n_schools and n_per_site; the earlier collapse with increasing n_per_site disappears.
  • The intercept and school-level covariates are somewhat lower at 15 sites (roughly 0.84-0.88) and approach 1 as the number of sites increases, which is consistent with ordinary small-site behavior rather than an n_per_site-driven collapse.
  • Child-intercept and residual variance estimates are essentially unbiased across the grid. School-intercept variance has positive bias at 15 sites (about 23-32%), decreasing to about 5-9% by 60 sites; this is a variance-component estimation pattern, not fixed-effect SE mis-calibration.
  • Conclusion: once each replicate draws fresh school effects, child effects, and residual errors from the fitted DGP, while the covariate design is held fixed and no rows are resampled, the severe synthetic fixed-effect SE discrepancy disappears. The earlier synthetic results were measuring a different procedure and should be replaced by these direct-DGP results.

7 Hybrid plasmode simulation (BLUP-resampled random effects)

7.1 Motivation and method

The direct-DGP synthetic simulations above draw school and child random effects from a Normal distribution with variance equal to the fitted variance component. This section tests a middle ground between that fully parametric approach and the real-data plasmode bootstrap: keep the fixed covariate design and residual-error generation exactly as in the direct-DGP synthetic simulation, but generate the school and child random effects by resampling with replacement from the model’s BLUPs (lme4::ranef(), the estimated random-effect means) instead of drawing from a Normal distribution.

Raw BLUPs are shrunk toward zero relative to the true random-effect variance (a well-known property of best linear unbiased prediction), so each BLUP pool is first centered to exactly mean zero and then rescaled so its variance equals the corresponding fitted variance component before any resampling: \[b^*_i = (b_i - \bar b) \times \sqrt{\hat\sigma^2 / \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(b - \bar b)}\] For Model A fit to the real data: the 60 school BLUPs have raw variance 0.056 (fitted var_schoolid = 0.079, so rescale factor \(\approx 1.19\)); the 1721 child BLUPs have raw variance 0.562 (fitted var_childid:schoolid = 0.652, rescale factor \(\approx 1.08\)). Each replicate then draws the school effect for every generated site (with replacement, from the rescaled 60-value school-BLUP pool) and the child effect for every generated child (with replacement, from the rescaled 1721-value child-BLUP pool); residual errors are still drawn fresh from \(N(0,\hat\sigma_e^2)\) as in the direct-DGP synthetic simulation. No rows of the real data are resampled – only the (rescaled) random-effect values are. Both grids are rerun with this design: tests/test_egsingle_hybrid_plasmode.R (n_schools in {15,30,60,90,120}) and tests/test_egsingle_hybrid_plasmode_fixed_n.R (n_schools in {15,30,60} x n_per_site in {25,50,100,200}), nsim = 1000 each.

7.3 Interpretation

  • Fixed-effect SE calibration matches the direct-DGP synthetic results. Across both grids, se_ratio is approximately 0.84-1.05 for every fixed effect, with no collapse as n_per_site increases – the severe mis-calibration seen under full bootstrap resampling of the real data (see the note near the top of this report) does not appear here, even though random effects are now drawn by resampling (with replacement) rather than from a Normal distribution.
  • var_schoolid_(Intercept) bias also matches the direct-DGP pattern: positive and shrinking with n_schools (about 31% at 15 sites down to about 5% at 120 sites, or 5-6% at 60 sites across all n_per_site values), essentially flat across n_per_site – not the negative, growing-with-n_schools pattern seen under full bootstrap resampling.
  • var_childid:schoolid_(Intercept) and var_Residual remain well calibrated (a few tenths of a percent) across both grids.
  • Conclusion: resampling with replacement from a rescaled finite pool of BLUPs behaves like drawing from the underlying Normal distribution for this purpose – it does not reproduce the full-bootstrap plasmode’s fixed-effect SE collapse or its sign-flipped, n_schools-growing var_schoolid bias. This indicates those full-bootstrap-specific patterns come from resampling entire rows/clusters of the real, finite dataset (with their attendant duplication of full covariate-and-residual blocks, and the unmodeled cross-level slope heterogeneity that comes along with them per Simon’s hypothesis above), not merely from using a finite, resampled – as opposed to continuously distributed – source for the random effects. This is why the hybrid plasmode simulation is now the primary calibration validation method: it retains empirically estimated random effects while avoiding the unmodeled slope heterogeneity that a full bootstrap of the real rows reintroduces.

8 Open questions / next steps

  • Simon’s slope-heterogeneity hypothesis (see the note above) explains why full bootstrap resampling of the real data fails to produce consistent SEs, but has not been separately, directly confirmed for every affected term (it fully explains year’s mis-calibration in the earlier slope-heterogeneity diagnostic, but not the full extent of the child-level-covariate or var_schoolid patterns). The hybrid plasmode simulation sidesteps this by construction (fixed covariate design, so no unmodeled cross-level slope heterogeneity can enter) rather than requiring a full resolution of the hypothesis.
  • These findings are directly relevant to the open Goal 2 design question about the effective sample size n for L-RESI: a single “number of schools” (or “number of children”) scaling will not correctly calibrate SEs for all fixed effects simultaneously in this 3-level design; the correct unit plausibly differs by which level a covariate varies at.
  • Decide whether n_schools/n_per_site values that exceed the real pool size (60 schools; ~5-89 children per school) should be dropped from future hybrid-plasmode sweeps or are informative as-is.
